newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's National, Labour support rises in NBR poll.
newsitem.headline: NZ's National, Labour support rises in NBR poll.

text.p: The two parties vying to head a government after the October 12 election have improved their support, according to a poll released on Friday.
But protracted negotiations over the shape of the government do not seem to have significantly dented the support for nationalist New Zealand First which holds the balance of power.

The UMR-Insight poll, published in the weekly business newspaper the National Business Review, showed support for the caretaker conservative National government was 38 percent against 33.82 percent support at the election. Labour polled 30 percent against 28.19 percent in the election.
NZ First's support was down marginally at 12 percent from 13.36 percent and the Alliance was virtually unchanged at 10 percent against 10.10 percent at the election.
Free-market Act New Zealand held its election support of 6.1 percent, registering six percent in the NBR poll.
The biggest losers were the small parties which with the exception of United MP Peter Dunne, failed to win any seats at the election.
The morals-based Christian Coalition's support fell from 4.33 percent to three percent. All other parties combined polled only one percent support against just over four percent at the election.
NZ First is negotiating separately with National and Labour over the shape of the next government.
The poll also asked whether the election outcome was a good thing for New Zealand.
Some 39 percent said it was good, down from 45 percent in a similar poll shortly after the election.
Thirty-six percent, up ten percentage points, said it was bad.
A majority of National supporters -- 53 percent -- said it was bad against 28 percent who said it was good.

More Labour voters thought it was a good result (47 percent) than rejected the result (25 percent) but NZ First and Alliance voters overwhelmingly welcomed the result, with 65 percent and 62 percent respectively approving and only nine percent and 23 percent respectively feeling it was bad for the country.
The poll of 750 respondents was taken between November 15 and 17 and has a margin of error of 3.5 percent.
